name: Infective Endocarditis

veryLikely: Viridans group streptococci (native valve, subacute presentation)
Staphylococcus aureus (acute presentation, IV drug use)
likely: Coagulase-negative staphylococci (prosthetic valve, particularly early post-operative)
possible: HACEK organisms and other fastidious organisms (culture-negative endocarditis)
pathogens.why: Pathogen likelihood depends heavily on the clinical context: native valve subacute disease points toward viridans streptococci, acute presentations and IV drug use point toward S. aureus, and prosthetic valve infection (especially early) points toward coagulase-negative staphylococci - empiric choice should be tailored to this context pending blood culture results.

investigations.test: Blood cultures (≥3 sets from separate sites, before antibiotics)
investigations.why: The single most important diagnostic step - identifies the organism and is a major Duke criterion; false-negative cultures from premature antibiotics significantly complicate diagnosis and management.

investigations.test: Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE), followed by transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) if TTE inconclusive or high suspicion persists
investigations.why: Identifies vegetations, abscess, or valve destruction - a major Duke criterion and essential for surgical planning.
Screens for new conduction abnormalities (e.g., new heart block), which can indicate perivalvular abscess extension.
Supports overall assessment of inflammatory burden and any renal involvement (e.g., immune complex glomerulonephritis).

reason: a history of injection drug use

raises strong suspicion for infective endocarditis. Multiple blood cultures must be drawn before starting empiric antibiotics, since cultures drawn after antibiotic initiation may become falsely negative and complicate both diagnosis (Duke criteria) and subsequent targeted therapy.

clinicalPearls: IE spans a clinical continuum from acute to subacute, and the causative organism largely dictates the tempo: beta-hemolytic streptococci, S. aureus and pneumococci tend to produce an acute, rapidly destructive course, whereas viridans streptococci, enterococci, CoNS and HACEK organisms usually cause subacute disease (Bartonella, T. whipplei, C. burnetii and M. chimaera are exceptionally indolent).

Fever is present in 80-90% of cases and a heart murmur in 80-85%, but in subacute IE fever is typically low-grade (rarely above 39.4 C) and may be blunted altogether in elderly, severely debilitated, or renal-failure patients.
A new or worsening regurgitant murmur is heard in only 20-50% of cases; in acute IE on a previously normal valve a murmur may be absent at first but is ultimately detected in about 85%.

Classic peripheral stigmata (Janeway lesions, Osler nodes, Roth spots, subungual/splinter hemorrhages) appear in only about 2-15% of cases and have become infrequent with earlier diagnosis; their absence does not exclude IE.

Janeway lesions are nonsuppurative painless hemorrhagic macules of the palms/soles classically linked to prolonged subacute infection, whereas septic emboli (subungual hemorrhages, Osler nodes) mimicking these lesions are common in acute S. aureus IE.
Three independent predictors of embolization are S. aureus etiology, mobile vegetations larger than 10 mm, and involvement of the anterior mitral leaflet.

In people who inject drugs, 35-60% of IE is confined to the tricuspid valve and presents with fever but faint or absent murmur and no peripheral stigmata, often with septic pulmonary emboli (cough, pleuritic pain, nodular infiltrates).

S. aureus bacteremia carries an 8-14% prevalence of IE and high mortality, so echocardiography (high-quality TTE, preferably TEE) is recommended routinely; intracardiac device, emboli, 2 or more positive cultures, community acquisition, vertebral osteomyelitis or persistent bacteremia each raise IE risk and argue for early TEE.

About 12-17% of patients with E. faecalis bacteremia and about 7% with non-beta-hemolytic streptococcal bacteremia have IE, justifying echocardiographic screening when predictive features are present.

Up to half of arterial emboli precede the diagnosis of IE; embolic risk falls rapidly once effective antibiotics begin, so emboli occurring late during or after therapy do not by themselves indicate treatment failure.

In hemodynamically stable patients with suspected subacute IE, empirical antibiotics can reasonably be withheld initially to allow uncontaminated blood cultures, but patients with sepsis or deteriorating hemodynamics should be treated immediately after the first three culture sets are drawn.

Surgery is indicated (as a knowledge concept, distinct from antibiotic regimens) for optimal outcome when there is moderate-severe CHF/shock from valve dysfunction, paravalvular extension with abscess/fistula/heart block, persistent bacteremia without an extracardiac source despite 7-10 days of therapy, lack of effective antimicrobial therapy (fungal, Brucella, multidrug-resistant gram-negative), or an unstable partially dehisced prosthetic valve; it is strongly considered for large (>10 mm) hypermobile vegetations with prior embolus and valve dysfunction, very large (>30 mm) vegetations, S. aureus PVE with intracardiac complications, and relapse after optimal therapy. Removal of all hardware is recommended for established CIED-IE.
harrison.pathophysiology: The prototypic lesion is the vegetation - a mass of platelets, fibrin, microorganisms and scant inflammatory cells - usually on heart valves but also on the low-pressure side of a ventricular septal defect, on mural endocardium injured by aberrant blood jets or foreign bodies, or on intracardiac devices. Intact endothelium resists most bacteria; endothelial injury (e.g., at sites of high-velocity jet impact or on the low-pressure side of a structural lesion) permits direct infection by virulent organisms or formation of a sterile platelet-fibrin thrombus (nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis, NBTE) that becomes a nidus for bacterial seeding during transient bacteremia. NBTE is most often associated with mitral regurgitation, aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation, ventricular septal defects and complex congenital heart disease, and also arises from hypercoagulable states (marantic endocarditis of malignancy/chronic disease and the bland vegetations of SLE and antiphospholipid syndrome). Circulating organisms adhere via surface adhesins (MSCRAMMs) - fibronectin-binding proteins, S. aureus clumping factor, enterococcal Fss2/Ace/Ebp pili, streptococcal glucans/FimA; S. aureus can even invade intact endothelium via fibronectin-binding proteins and von Willebrand factor, allowing infection of previously normal valves. Adherent organisms proliferate into microcolonies, induce platelet deposition and a local procoagulant (tissue-factor) state, and become buried in fibrin; deep organisms are metabolically inactive and relatively antibiotic-resistant while surface organisms are continuously shed into the blood. Clinical manifestations arise from intracardiac structural damage, embolization of vegetation fragments causing remote infarction/infection, hematogenous seeding during bacteremia, and immune-complex deposition; constitutional symptoms reflect cytokine release.
additionalDifferentials: Marantic (nonbacterial thrombotic) endocarditis associated with malignancy and chronic wasting disease
Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome with bland valvular vegetations
Systemic lupus erythematosus with sterile (Libman-Sacks-type) vegetations
infectionMimics: Culture-negative IE due to fastidious organisms (Coxiella burnetii, Bartonella spp., Tropheryma whipplei, Brucella, nutritionally variant Granulicatella/Gemella/Abiotrophia, Corynebacterium/Cutibacterium acnes, Mycobacterium chimaera)
additionalInvestigations: Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) detects vegetations in over 90% of definite IE and is preferred over TTE, which misses vegetations under 2 mm and yields inadequate images in about 20% of patients; a negative TEE with high clinical suspicion should be repeated in 7-10 days.
Three-dimensional TEE to better define vegetations and perivalvular extension.
ECG-gated multislice cardiac CT angiography - superior to TEE for pseudoaneurysm/abscess and can assess coronary patency preoperatively; CTA findings count as a major imaging criterion.

18F-FDG-PET/CT - increases sensitivity in suspected prosthetic-valve IE (including TAVR-PVE), aortic graft, CIED pocket/lead and LVAD infection, and extracardiac foci; false positives within 3 months of valve surgery.

Molecular testing of excised/embolized vegetation: organism-specific PCR (C. burnetii, Bartonella, T. whipplei, C. acnes, M. hominis) and broad-range 16S (or 28S for fungi) rRNA PCR with sequencing; only moderately sensitive, so a negative result does not exclude IE.
Serologic/PCR testing for culture-negative pathogens: Coxiella burnetii (phase I IgG titer >=1:800) and Bartonella henselae/quintana (IgG titer >=1:800).
Brain MRI/MRA in any neurologic signs or symptoms (including unusual headache) to detect emboli, hemorrhage, or mycotic aneurysms.
Spine MRI for recalcitrant back pain or focal spinal tenderness to assess for vertebral osteomyelitis/spondylodiscitis and epidural abscess.
Routine adjunctive labs: CBC (anemia in 70-90%), ESR (elevated in 60-90%), CRP (elevated in over 90%), microscopic hematuria (30-50%), rheumatoid factor (~50%), creatinine and liver function tests.
redFlags: Congestive heart failure or pulmonary edema/cardiogenic shock from valve dysfunction or intracardiac fistula (develops in 30-40%) - a surgical emergency
New electrocardiographic conduction disturbance or new heart block, suggesting paravalvular/septal abscess extension
Cerebrovascular embolism (stroke or encephalopathy), which complicates 15-35% of cases
Intracranial hemorrhage from hemorrhagic infarct or ruptured mycotic aneurysm
Persistent fever or persistently positive blood cultures despite appropriate antibiotics, indicating uncontrolled infection
New or worsening regurgitant murmur or prosthetic valve dehiscence
Large (over 10 mm) mobile vegetation, particularly on the anterior mitral leaflet, with high embolic risk
Acute S. aureus or fungal IE, and any prosthetic-valve involvement
harrison.prognosis: Overall survival in developed countries is about 80-85%, but varies markedly by subgroup. About 85-90% survive NVE caused by viridans streptococci, HACEK organisms, or synergy-susceptible enterococci. Non-injecting patients with S. aureus NVE have 55-70% survival; injecting patients have 85-90%, but 1-year mortality rises to 20-30% if substance-use disorder is not addressed. Prosthetic-valve IE arising within 2 months of surgery carries 40-50% mortality versus only 10-20% for late-onset PVE; elderly TAVR-PVE in-hospital mortality is 35-50%, rising to 60-75% at 1 year. Crude survival after successful treatment is roughly 80-90% at 1 year and 70-80% at 2 years. Death often reflects comorbidities and end-organ complications rather than antibiotic failure. Adverse outcomes are linked to older age, severe comorbidity/diabetes, delayed diagnosis, prosthetic or aortic valve involvement, virulent or resistant pathogens (S. aureus, P. aeruginosa, yeast), intracardiac and major neurologic complications, and health care-associated infection.
pitfalls: Relying on a new/worsening murmur alone - it is a physical-exam minor criterion only; a major imaging criterion requires echocardiographic evidence of new valvular regurgitation, not auscultation.

Treating a negative TTE (or even a negative initial TEE) as ruling out IE; TTE misses vegetations under 2 mm and is poor for prosthetic valves, and initial TEE is falsely negative in 6-18% (especially TAVR-PVE) - repeat in 7-10 days when suspicion persists.
Forgetting that 5-15% of IE is blood-culture negative, often because of prior antibiotics; withholding empirical therapy when stable preserves diagnostic yield.
Interpreting persistent organism DNA detected in excised valves (in ~45% of patients who completed therapy) as antibiotic failure - relapse after surgery for active IE is actually uncommon.
Misattributing emboli that occur late during or after effective therapy to treatment failure.
Overlooking that prior antibiotics within 2 weeks blunt culture yield and that nontypical organisms require 3 or more positive sets (plus no extracardiac focus) to count as a major criterion.
Assuming antithrombotic therapy prevents systemic emboli in NVE - it does not.
harrison.severityClassification: Diagnosis uses the 2023 Duke-International Society for Cardiovascular Infectious Diseases (Duke-ISCVID) update of the modified Duke criteria (sensitivity 80-93%). MAJOR criteria: (1) Microbiologic - a typical IE organism in 2 or more separate blood culture sets (S. aureus, S. lugdunensis, E. faecalis, all streptococci except S. pneumoniae and S. pyogenes, Granulicatella/Abiotrophia/Gemella, HACEK group; and, when intracardiac prosthetic material is present, CoNS, C. striatum, C. jeikeium, S. marcescens, P. aeruginosa, C. acnes, nontuberculous mycobacteria and Candida), OR a nontypical organism in 3 or more sets; positive PCR/single culture/serology for C. burnetii, Bartonella spp. or T. whipplei. (2) Imaging - echocardiography or cardiac CT showing vegetation, perforation/leaflet aneurysm, abscess, pseudoaneurysm or fistula, OR new valvular regurgitation, OR new prosthetic dehiscence; OR abnormal FDG-PET/CT activity on a valve/graft/lead/prosthetic material. (3) Surgical - IE seen at direct surgical inspection. MINOR criteria: predisposing condition (prior IE, injection drug use, prosthetic valve, prior valve repair, congenital heart disease such as bicuspid aortic valve, CIED, more-than-mild regurgitation/stenosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy); fever over 38.0 C; vascular phenomena (arterial emboli, septic pulmonary infarcts, mycotic aneurysm, intracranial/conjunctival hemorrhage, Janeway lesions); immunologic phenomena (glomerulonephritis, Osler nodes, Roth spots, positive rheumatoid factor); microbiologic evidence not meeting a major criterion; and PET/CT activity within 3 months of prosthetic implantation. CLASSIFICATION: DEFINITE IE = pathologic confirmation OR 2 major, or 1 major + 3 minor, or 5 minor criteria. POSSIBLE IE = 1 major + 1 minor, or 3 minor. REJECTED = firm alternative diagnosis, or resolution with under 4 days of antibiotics, or no histologic evidence at surgery/autopsy after under 4 days of therapy. IE is also classified by tempo (acute vs subacute), site (native vs prosthetic valve, right-sided/tricuspid), cause, and predisposition (injection drug use, health care-associated).
